lines.text: Myth (2026): "full coverage" car insurance covers everything. It doesn't.
lines.say: Full coverage car insurance? It doesn't cover everything.

lines.text: And it isn't cheap: Bankrate's 2026 national average for full coverage is $2,697 a year.
lines.say: It's not cheap: Bankrate's twenty twenty-six average is about twenty-seven hundred dollars a year.

lines.text: "Full coverage" has no official definition. It usually means liability + collision + comprehensive.
lines.say: But full coverage isn't an official policy. It usually means liability, collision and comprehensive.

lines.text: Liability has limits. Common state minimum 25/50/25: $25,000 per person, $50,000 per crash, $25,000 property.
lines.say: Liability has limits: a common state minimum is twenty-five, fifty, twenty-five, in thousands.

lines.text: Usually not included: the loan gap, rental and towing (unless added), wear and tear, rideshare driving.
lines.say: Bills above that aren't covered. Also missing: the loan gap, rentals, towing, wear and tear, and rideshare driving.

lines.text: Example: a totaled car worth $20,000 (actual cash value) with $25,000 still owed on the loan.
lines.say: Example: the car's totaled. It's worth twenty thousand dollars, and the loan is twenty-five thousand.

lines.text: In 2023, 15.4% of US drivers (about 1 in 7) were uninsured (Insurance Research Council). Uninsured motorist coverage is a separate line.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-three, about one in seven drivers had no insurance. Uninsured motorist coverage is separate.

lines.text: "Full coverage" = three coverages. Gap, rental, towing, rideshare and uninsured motorist are separate lines on the policy.
lines.say: So full coverage means three coverages. The rest are separate lines.

post.title: Myth: "full coverage" car insurance covers everything
post.ig:
"Full coverage" car insurance doesn't cover everything.

"Full coverage" has no official definition: it usually means liability + collision + comprehensive. Bankrate's 2026 national average: $2,697 a year.
A common state liability minimum is 25/50/25 ($25,000 per person, $50,000 per crash, $25,000 property). Bills above the limits aren't covered.
Usually not included: the loan gap, rental and towing unless added, wear and tear, rideshare driving.
Example: car worth $20,000, $25,000 loan, $500 deductible: payout $19,500, still owed $5,500. In 2023, 15.4% of drivers (about 1 in 7) were uninsured.

Sources: Bankrate (2026); West Virginia Insurance Commissioner; Insurance Research Council (2023 data); CNBC Select.
